findings.title: On Windows a tagged group has no current memory figure from the kernel, so the brief's claim that the kernel provides 'CPU time, memory, I/O' totals is false for memory
findings.evidence: docs/17-build-prompt.md:62 says 'The kernel's totals for the group are authoritative: CPU time, memory, I/O and process counts'. 05-data-flow.md:52 says 'the kernel totals CPU, memory and I/O'. 09-telemetry.md:9 marks tagged totals as 'Full'. Re-fetched Microsoft Learn: JOBOBJECT_BASIC_ACCOUNTING_INFORMATION has TotalUserTime, TotalKernelTime, ThisPeriod*, TotalPageFaultCount, TotalProcesses, ActiveProcesses and TotalTerminatedProcesses, and no memory member. JOBOBJECT_EXTENDED_LIMIT_INFORMATION has only peaks: 'PeakProcessMemoryUsed: The peak memory used by any process ever associated with the job.' and 'PeakJobMemoryUsed: The peak memory usage of all processes currently associated with the job.' Its limits are commit ('virtual memory that can be committed'). JOBOBJECT_LIMIT_VIOLATION_INFORMATION.JobMemory is filled only 'If the ViolationLimitFlags member specifies JOB_OBJECT_LIMIT_JOB_MEMORY ... at the time the notification was sent', which needs a limit, and 17:69 forbids limits. None of the other 15 classes in the QueryInformationJobObject table returns memory. The brief contradicts itself: 17:81 says 'Workload totals use USS', and 10-known-limits.md:18 says workload memory 'can lag by up to the USS interval'. 17:66 ('accounted for even if the collector was not running') and 17:127 ('peak and mean memory') cannot both hold for memory.
findings.impact: The brief tells the builder to read tagged-workload memory from a Windows source that does not exist. Taking PeakJobMemoryUsed would show peak commit as current memory, in a different unit from the USS used for polled workloads. Otherwise the brief gives tagged memory no stated source. A run file the launcher writes while the collector is down cannot contain mean memory.
findings.proposed_change: docs/17-build-prompt.md:62: 'On Windows the job provides CPU time, I/O and process counts, including exited processes, plus peak commit (PeakJobMemoryUsed), and no current memory. Current memory for a tagged group is the sum of USS over its members (JobObjectBasicProcessIdList), shown with the age of the reading like any other workload.' 05-data-flow.md:52: 'the kernel totals CPU and I/O'. 09-telemetry.md row 'Tagged workload totals': 'CPU, I/O, process counts: full. Memory: peak commit only; current memory from per-process reads.' 17:127: mean memory comes from the collector's samples and is unavailable for a run the collector never saw; a peak taken from the job is labelled peak commit.
findings.cost: About five sentences across three documents
findings.verification: Re-fetched four Microsoft pages: QueryInformationJobObject, BASIC_ACCOUNTING, EXTENDED_LIMIT and LIMIT_VIOLATION. Their quotes hold, and no documented class returns current job memory. Searched docs/ and found 17:81 and 10:18, which already point to USS, so the brief contradicts itself rather than having no answer. R01, R06 and R15 do not cover this. Downgraded from critical to high. A wrong number appears only if the builder labels peak commit as current memory, and priority 1, 17:81 and AGENTS.md ('say so and ask') steer against that. What is certain is a false statement in the spec and a run-file promise that cannot be met. The Linux cgroup memory.current is a different unit from PSS; that belongs to the Linux batch.

findings.title: A job's name disappears when its last handle closes, so a collector that is the only holder cannot re-open it by name after a restart; the brief offers that option, contrary to R15
findings.evidence: Re-fetched Job Objects: 'Only named job objects can be opened.' and 'The job is destroyed when its last handle has been closed and all associated processes have been terminated.' Re-fetched Life Cycle of an Object: 'A temporary object can be accessed by name only as long as its handle count is nonzero. Once the handle count decrements to zero, the object's name is removed from the object manager's namespace.' docs/17-build-prompt.md:67: 'a small detached holder, or the collector. Choose one and test it.' R15's fix (16-review-log.md:147): 'held open by a detached helper until the group is empty'. P2 gate 17:270 and 15:17: 'a restarted collector re-attaches to live groups'. AssignProcessToJobObject (re-fetched): 'All processes within a job must run within the same session as the job.'
findings.impact: If the collector holds the only handle, a collector restart after `submeter run` has returned leaves the job alive with no name. Re-attach fails, that run's totals (including exited children) are lost, and the P2 gate fails. The brief leaves the choice open, although R15 already chose a helper.
findings.proposed_change: docs/17-build-prompt.md:67: replace 'a small detached holder, or the collector. Choose one and test it.' with 'a small detached holder that keeps a handle until ActiveProcesses is 0 and then writes the final totals. Not the collector: on Windows a job can be opened by name only while some handle to it is open, so a restarted collector could not find it. If no handle survives, record the run's totals as lost, never as zero. The launcher, the holder and the collector run in the same logon session.'
findings.cost: Two or three sentences in one document
findings.verification: Re-fetched both Microsoft pages; the quotes are present and mean what the lead says. Confirmed that the brief (17:67) differs from R15's fix, so R15 does not resolve it. Found no documented way to get a job handle from a member process; IsProcessInJob only tests membership. Mitigating: a builder who chose the collector would fail the P2 gate, so the cost is rework rather than a silently wrong number. The severity stays high because the brief offers an option that fails a gate. I dropped the lead's Global\ prefix suggestion, because the same-session rule above is enough.

findings.title: With breakaway forbidden, a program that runs directly in a tagged job and asks for CREATE_BREAKAWAY_FROM_JOB, or that puts a child in a job with UI limits, fails under submeter run; allowing breakaway may lose Node agents' grandchildren
findings.evidence: docs/17-build-prompt.md:69: 'Do not allow breakaway'. 17:23: 'Placing a process tree ... into a Job Object ... for accounting is allowed. Setting any limit on that group is not.' Re-fetched Process Creation Flags, CREATE_BREAKAWAY_FROM_JOB: 'If the calling process is associated with a job, the job must set the JOB_OBJECT_LIMIT_BREAKAWAY_OK limit.' Re-fetched libuv src/win/process.c: 'CREATE_BREAKAWAY_FROM_JOB makes the CreateProcess call fail if we're under job control that doesn't allow breakaway.' libuv's own job sets LimitFlags = BREAKAWAY_OK | SILENT_BREAKAWAY_OK | DIE_ON_UNHANDLED_EXCEPTION | KILL_ON_JOB_CLOSE. Re-fetched AssignProcessToJobObject: the target job 'cannot have UI limits set', and 'The child process breaks away from every job in the job chain unless a job in the chain does not allow breakaway. In this case, the child process does not break away from that job or any job above it'. Re-fetched Nested Jobs: a breakaway moves 'up the hierarchy until it reaches a job that does not permit breakaway.'
findings.impact: A program that requests breakaway from inside the tagged job, or that nests its own UI-limited job, behaves differently only when launched through Submeter. How many programs do this is undocumented. The text of fixed rule 1 is not broken: it lists priority, affinity, suspend, kill and memory cap; 17:23 allows job placement; and forbidding breakaway is the job's default, not a limit. Counter-risk to the leads' fix: Node (libuv) puts each child into its own job with SILENT_BREAKAWAY_OK, so grandchildren such as bash, git and rg break away and move up the chain. Today Submeter's job stops them. If that job set BREAKAWAY_OK, it is undocumented whether those silent breakaways also leave it. If they do, Node-based agents, the main use case, lose their children from exact accounting. Setting BREAKAWAY_OK is also a LimitFlags value, which 17:23 forbids as written.
findings.proposed_change: Owner ruling first. Recommended: keep 'Do not allow breakaway'. Add a row to docs/10-known-limits.md: 'A program that asks to break away from a tagged group, or that places children in its own job with UI limits, cannot start those children under submeter run.' Add a Windows test to P0 (windows-priorities.md item 7) and to the P2 gate: (a) a direct child calls CreateProcess with CREATE_BREAKAWAY_FROM_JOB, record the error; (b) node, then bash, then a grandchild, and the grandchild stays in the group; (c) a Chromium-based browser started in a tagged run opens pages. Consider BREAKAWAY_OK only if (b) still holds with it set.
findings.cost: One table row and one gate clause, after the ruling
findings.decision_question: Tagged Windows groups: (1) keep breakaway forbidden, so exact totals include all of Node's grandchildren, but a program that requests breakaway fails under submeter run; or (2) set JOB_OBJECT_LIMIT_BREAKAWAY_OK (never SILENT), so those programs behave as they would without Submeter, but silent breakaways from libuv's job might then escape the tagged group (undocumented), and 17:23 'no limits' would need an exception. Recommendation: (1), with the known-limits row, plus the Windows test in P0 that decides whether (2) is safe.
findings.verification: Re-fetched four Microsoft pages and the libuv source. The quotes are present. The nested-chain rule in AssignProcessToJobObject narrows the failure to processes whose immediate job is Submeter's. It also brought to light libuv's SILENT_BREAKAWAY_OK job, which neither lead mentions and which makes their recommended fix risky. Downgraded from high to medium: no fixed rule is broken by its text, node/libuv itself never requests breakaway, and which programs are affected is suspected (would confirm: test (c) above). Chromium is the likeliest case, because of its UI-limited sandbox jobs.

findings.title: The brief does not say how the command enters the job; with Popen followed by AssignProcessToJobObject, early children escape the group, and the CREATE_SUSPENDED workaround invites a dispute under rule 1
findings.evidence: Re-fetched Job Objects: 'After a process is associated with a job, by default any child processes it creates using CreateProcess are also associated with the job.' CPython 3.14.5 subprocess.py:1553 has `hp, ht, pid, tid = _winapi.CreateProcess(...)`, and :1574-1576 keeps _handle and pid, calls `_winapi.CloseHandle(ht)`, and discards tid. In subprocess.py:206 and :209-211, STARTUPINFO.lpAttributeList carries only handle_list. Re-fetched UpdateProcThreadAttribute: 'PROC_THREAD_ATTRIBUTE_JOB_LIST: The lpValue parameter is a pointer to a list of job handles to be assigned to the child process ... Supported in Windows 10 and newer'. AssignProcessToJobObject remarks point to CREATE_SUSPENDED. docs/17:62 and 13-build-list.md:23 say what the launcher does, not how. AGENTS.md:9 lists 'suspend' under rule 1.
findings.impact: A command that spawns at once (a shell running git or rg) can start children before the assignment. Their CPU is missing from the 'exact' total in the spawn-heavy case R01 exists for. The P2 gate compares against the same kernel total, so it cannot notice. Creating the command suspended and resuming it needs ctypes anyway, and reviewers may read it as a breach of rule 1.
findings.proposed_change: docs/17-build-prompt.md after :62: 'On Windows the launcher creates the command inside the job with PROC_THREAD_ATTRIBUTE_JOB_LIST through CreateProcessW (ctypes), so no descendant is born outside the group and nothing is created suspended. If the launcher instead joins the job itself before starting the command, it must start the detached holder first, because a process in a job that forbids breakaway can never leave it.' Add the same rule for the cgroup path in docs/13 component 13 (Linux detail belongs to the Linux batch).
findings.verification: Read the subprocess.py lines on this machine's 3.14.5 standard library and re-fetched both Microsoft pages; the claims hold. Searched docs 05, 09, 13, 14 and 17 for a launch sequence and found none. The width of the race is unmeasured (no Windows), so it stays medium. New detail: G's 'launcher joins the job itself' alternative conflicts with the holder. A holder started after the join sits inside the job, which forbids breakaway, so ActiveProcesses never reaches 0 unless the holder counts itself. The proposed text says how to avoid that.

findings.title: Nested tagged runs double count: an outer job's kernel totals include every inner job's processes, and the brief has no rule to subtract them
findings.evidence: Re-fetched Nested Jobs: 'Resource accounting information for a nested job describes the usage of every process associated with that job, including processes in child jobs.' Re-fetched AssignProcessToJobObject: 'Accounting information is added to the immediate job and aggregated in each parent job in the job chain.' docs/17-build-prompt.md:62 treats group totals as authoritative. :94 says 'Every process maps to exactly one workload, in this order: kernel group membership', but does not say which of two groups wins. :127 says run summaries hold 'exact totals'. In docs/, 'nested' appears only at 03-cli-output.md:53 ('nested jobs available'); there is no subtraction rule and the run file has no parent field.
findings.impact: Example: `submeter run --as ide -- code`, then `submeter run --as agent:x -- claude` from the IDE's terminal. The ide run's kernel totals include the agent's work, so cost and diff charge it twice. Reconciliation (17:98) catches the excess only when the inner share is above 2% of capacity; smaller inner runs pass silently.
findings.proposed_change: docs/17-build-prompt.md, Collection: 'If submeter run starts inside a tagged group (the outer launcher sets SUBMETER_RUN_ID in the command's environment, and the inner launcher reads its own environment), the run file records the parent run. A process belongs to its innermost group. A parent's reported totals are its kernel totals minus its tagged children's totals, so each CPU-second belongs to one workload.' P2 gate (17:270, 15:17): a nested tagged run reconciles within 2%, and the parent's run total excludes the child.
findings.cost: Three sentences and one gate clause
findings.verification: Re-fetched both pages; the quotes hold. Searched docs/ for nested, inner and parent-group handling and found none. Upgraded from medium to high: following the brief as written gives a double-counted, wrong number whenever runs nest, silently below 2%. Not critical, because nesting needs a deliberate usage the brief does not describe. Linux cgroup v2 is also hierarchical if inner groups are created under outer ones (not checked here).

findings.title: The psutil fallback is not independent of the bulk snapshot: CPU times, start time and I/O sit in Reserved members, psutil reaches the same call for thread counts and denied processes, and it makes one whole-system query per process per snapshot
findings.evidence: Re-fetched NtQuerySystemInformation: '[NtQuerySystemInformation may be altered or unavailable in future versions of Windows...]'. The SYSTEM_PROCESS_INFORMATION layout shows 'BYTE Reserved1[48];' after NumberOfThreads and 'LARGE_INTEGER Reserved7[6];' at the end, and 'The other members of the structure are reserved for internal use by the operating system.' Probe docs/review/probes/verify-3/w6_thread_queries.out.txt (psutil 7.2.2): '_proc_info calls: [cext.proc_info]'; 'num_threads reaches _proc_info: True (on the only path)'; create_time, cpu_times and io_counters reach it in except fallbacks; oneshot_enter caches per Process; 'snapshot 1: 466 processes returned ... num_threads called 467 times'. psutil_provider.py:64 calls num_threads for every process. docs/17:71 and R17 (16-review-log.md:155-159) present psutil as the fallback.
findings.impact: If the structure changes, the fallback is hit as well: thread counts and every process the user cannot open go through the same call. On Windows the fallback makes about N whole-system queries of N entries each per snapshot, so it is the costliest path exactly when it is in use. Today PsutilProvider is the baseline's only provider, so `submeter top` on Windows already runs this path.
findings.proposed_change: docs/17-build-prompt.md:71, plus a note under R17 in docs/16-review-log.md: 'CPU times, start time and I/O are members Microsoft documents only as Reserved, and psutil's Windows path uses the same call for thread counts and for processes it cannot open, so the fallback reduces the dependency but does not remove it. The CI parse test is the guard.' src/submeter/providers/psutil_provider.py:64: on Windows do not call num_threads, and record threads as unavailable (ProcessCounters.threads becomes int | None).
findings.cost: Two doc sentences; about 5-8 lines in the provider and core/models.py
findings.verification: Re-fetched the Microsoft page (the Reserved layout holds). Wrote and ran my own AST and runtime probe; it confirms num_threads goes to _proc_info and cext.proc_info, with the cache per Process only, one call per process per snapshot. Downgraded from high to medium. The parse risk itself is R17's and already has a CI guard. windows-priorities.md item 3 already warns that psutil will miss the 10 ms target, so P0 will not misread the cost. The quadratic cost applies only while the fallback runs and its size is unmeasured (no Windows). No gate fails as such.

findings.title: daemon install's Windows scheduled task is unspecified; with Task Scheduler defaults it will not start on battery, stops on unplug, is killed after 72 h and runs at below-normal priority; whether a standard user can register it is unsettled
findings.evidence: Re-fetched TaskSettings pages. DisallowStartIfOnBatteries: 'If True, the task will not be started if the computer is running on batteries... The default is True.' StopIfGoingOnBatteries: 'will be stopped if the computer is going onto batteries... The default is True.' ExecutionTimeLimit: 'By default, a task will be stopped 72 hours after it starts to run.' and 'A value of PT0S will enable the task to run indefinitely.' Priority: 'The default value is 7.', and 7 maps to BELOW_NORMAL_PRIORITY_CLASS. Re-fetched schtasks create: 'Only Administrators can schedule tasks, regardless of the value of the /ru parameter.' appears under 'To schedule a task that runs with system permissions'; the Remarks say 'Schtasks always prompts for a password unless you provide one, even when you schedule a task on the local computer using the current user account.' docs/17:199 and 13-build-list.md:48 name the task with no settings; 08-configuration.md:71 on_battery_multiplier shows the collector is meant to run on battery.
findings.impact: A task created with defaults leaves gaps in the trend data on a work laptop (on battery, after unplugging, after 72 h of uptime). It starves the collector under the CPU load that live diagnosis is for. Soaks on mains power under 72 h pass anyway. Fixed rule 2 is at risk if a standard user cannot register a logon task for themselves, or if registration stores a password (suspected).
findings.proposed_change: docs/17-build-prompt.md:199: 'On Windows, daemon install registers a task for the current user only: a logon trigger with LogonType InteractiveToken (runs only while the user is signed in, stores no password), DisallowStartIfOnBatteries=false, StopIfGoingOnBatteries=false, ExecutionTimeLimit=PT0S, MultipleInstancesPolicy=IgnoreNew, restart on failure, and Priority 5 (normal). If phase 0 shows a standard user cannot register it, use HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run instead. doctor reads these settings back.' windows-priorities.md item 7: add 'register and delete a logon task as a standard user'.
findings.cost: One paragraph and one checklist line
findings.decision_question: The task's priority: keep the Task Scheduler default of 7 (below normal; the collector starves under load), or set 5 (normal, the same as any program the user starts)? Setting Submeter's own priority does not change an observed process, but rule 1 names 'priority'. Recommendation: 5, with a sentence that rule 1 covers observed processes, not Submeter itself.
findings.verification: Re-fetched five Microsoft pages; every default quoted is present. Searched docs/ for battery, 72 h and execution-limit handling; only 17:199 and 13:48 mention the task, with no settings. The administrators sentence sits in the System-account section, so the rule 2 part stays suspected (would confirm: as a standard user, Register-ScheduledTask with an AtLogOn trigger for $env:USERNAME and LogonType Interactive, then delete it). I did not re-fetch the performance-counter interactive-logon point; InteractiveToken makes it moot. High rests on the verified defaults.

findings.title: One-instance lock on Windows: the OS may release a dead holder's lock late and acquire() tries once; platform_check waits a fixed 0.5 s; a test reads the locked byte through a second handle; holder() reports a dead pid
findings.evidence: Re-fetched LockFile: 'If a process terminates with a portion of a file locked ... the locks are unlocked by the operating system. However, the time it takes for the operating system to unlock these locks depends upon available system resources.' and 'If the locking process opens the file a second time, it cannot access the specified region through this second handle until it unlocks the region.' files.py:219-231: one _try_lock call, then return False. Probe verify-3/w8_lock_attempts.out.txt: 'acquire() returned False after 1 attempt(s)'; 'holder() returns that pid: True; a process with that pid exists now: False'. Re-ran e-baseline/lock_cases.py with the same result. platform_check.py:53-55: kill, wait, sleep(0.5), then one retry. tests/test_baseline.py:329 and platform_check.py:52 call read_bytes() on the lock file from the locking process while byte 0 is locked.
findings.impact: A collector restarted right after a crash or a Task Manager kill can exit with 'another copy is already running', leaving no collector. platform_check can print a false FAIL. If Windows refuses Python's read at offset 0 (readall asks for size+1 bytes, which overlaps the locked byte), test_file_map_names_expiry_and_lock fails on Windows and check_lock crashes, blocking the P0 gate (suspected). holder() names a dead pid after a crash; nothing outside the tests calls it yet.
findings.proposed_change: src/submeter/store/files.py InstanceLock.acquire(): when refused, retry every 100 ms for up to 5 s. holder(): return None when a non-blocking try-lock succeeds. tests/test_baseline.py:329 and scripts/platform_check.py:52: check emptiness with stat().st_size == 0 instead of read_bytes(). platform_check.py:55: poll for up to 5 s instead of one 0.5 s sleep.
findings.would_confirm: On Windows: with the lock held by this process, Path(lock).read_bytes() through a new handle; PermissionError [WinError 33] confirms the test failure. Also kill a holder and loop acquire() every 10 ms over 50 trials to measure time to release.
findings.verification: Re-fetched LockFile; both quotes hold. Wrote a probe counting _try_lock calls and a stale-pid case, and re-ran the E probe. The no-retry behaviour and the stale pid are verified on Linux from the code. The locked-read part stays suspected: the documentation does not say whether a read at EOF counts as accessing the locked region. windows-priorities.md:37 already knows another program cannot read a locked byte, but the test reads through a second handle in the same process. Kept medium (misleading check results, a refused restart), not high, because the gate failure is unconfirmed.

findings.title: psutil reads command lines through the PEB with more access than needed, once per process per sample; on managed machines Defender's LSASS ASR rule may log it
findings.evidence: psutil _pswindows.py:763-775: cmdline() tries the PEB first ('PEB method detects cmdline changes but requires more privileges') and falls back on a permission error. psutil_provider.py:69 calls cmdline() for every process on every snapshot, and platform_check.py:77-92 runs 41 snapshots. Re-fetched ASR rules reference: the rule is under 'Standard protection rules'. 'Some apps enumerate all running processes and attempt to open them with exhaustive permissions. This ASR rule denies the app's open process actions and records the details to the Security log in Windows Event Viewer. This rule can generate numerous noise.' Also: 'This activity generates considerable ASR rule noise, but doesn't block functionality.' The EDR alerts column for the rule is 'N'. 'If you enabled Local Security Authority (LSA) protection ... This ASR rule isn't required.' windows-priorities.md:89: 'If a probe is flagged, stop and tell me.'
findings.impact: No number, fixed rule or job is affected: per Microsoft the rule logs and does not block functionality, and raises no EDR alert. The risk is audit events naming python.exe on a managed computer, which would trigger the owner's stop rule in P0 and draw IT attention. Reading command lines every sample also adds avoidable per-process opens.
findings.proposed_change: docs/17-build-prompt.md:71: 'Open other processes with PROCESS_QUERY_LIMITED_INFORMATION only, never PROCESS_VM_READ, and read command lines with NtQueryInformationProcess (ProcessCommandLineInformation) once per new process, not per sample.' windows-priorities.md item 7: 'after platform_check, look in the Defender Operational log for ASR events naming python.exe.'
findings.would_confirm: On a Windows machine with the ASR LSASS rule in audit or block mode and LSA protection off, run platform_check, then search the Defender Operational log and the AsrLsassCredentialTheftAudited/Blocked hunting events for python.exe.
findings.verification: Re-read the psutil source and the provider. Re-fetched the ASR page; the quotes hold, but the same page says the rule 'doesn't block functionality', has no EDR alert, and is not required where LSA protection is on. So I downgraded from medium to low. Still suspected: undocumented whether a standard user's open of lsass, which its DACL refuses, reaches the ASR callback at all. Did not re-check event IDs 1121/1122, so I left them out of the proposal.

findings.title: Windows private bytes come from psutil's 'private' alias with a silent getattr fallback to working set
findings.evidence: psutil_provider.py:63: `int(getattr(memory, "private", memory.rss))`. Probe verify-3/w10_private_fallback.out.txt: 'without private: provider kept 111000000 (rss is 111000000, vms is 333000000); warnings: none; fell back to working set silently: True'. pyproject.toml:8 'psutil>=6.0' has no upper bound; uv.lock pins 7.2.2. The PyPI JSON shows latest release 7.2.2, so psutil 8 is unreleased. psutil.io/api (dev docs), 8.0.0 changelog: 'pagefile and private -> vms' and 'All these old names still work but raise DeprecationWarning.' psutil 7.2.2 _pswindows.py:819 has `vms = t[7]  # pagefile`. Re-fetched PROCESS_MEMORY_COUNTERS_EX: 'PrivateUsage: Same as PagefileUsage.'
findings.impact: Nothing breaks at the next relock: in 8.0 the alias still works and only warns. A later release that removes it would switch Windows memory to working set with no error, bringing back the R06 failure that leak detection was designed to avoid.
findings.proposed_change: src/submeter/providers/psutil_provider.py:63: on Windows read memory.vms (PagefileUsage, which equals PrivateUsage, in psutil 7.x; mapped to PrivateUsage in 8.x), and memory.rss elsewhere, with no getattr fallback.
findings.verification: Wrote and ran a probe that replaces psutil's platform memory_info and shows the silent fallback. Checked PyPI and the psutil dev docs: the lead's 'psutil 8 deprecates' refers to an unreleased version that keeps the alias with a warning, so the risk is further off than stated. Found a simpler fix than version branching: vms is already private bytes on Windows in both 7.x and 8.x (Microsoft: PrivateUsage is 'Same as PagefileUsage').
